clinicalPearls: SPG55 is an autosomal recessive childhood-onset complicated HSP caused by biallelic mutations in C12orf65 (renamed MTRFR), which encodes a mitochondrial translation release / rescue factor.
The molecular defect impairs mitochondrial protein synthesis, producing a combined deficiency of the oxidative-phosphorylation respiratory-chain complexes.
The hallmark is spastic paraplegia combined with optic atrophy and reduced visual acuity and an axonal sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy.
Distal amyotrophy is common, and some patients develop external ophthalmoplegia or ptosis.
C12orf65 / MTRFR disease is a spectrum: the same gene causes combined oxidative-phosphorylation deficiency type 7 and Leigh-like encephalopathy at the severe end.
The phenotype overlaps that of Behr syndrome (childhood optic atrophy with spasticity, ataxia and neuropathy).
It should be considered alongside SPG7 as one of the mitochondrial hereditary spastic paraplegias.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG55 is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in C12orf65, located on chromosome 12q24.31 and now designated MTRFR (mitochondrial translation release factor in rescue). Its protein product is a matrix member of the mitochondrial release-factor family that does not itself terminate normal translation but rescues stalled mitochondrial ribosomes by hydrolysing the bond between peptidyl-tRNA and the stalled nascent chain, freeing ribosomal subunits for reuse. When this quality-control step fails, synthesis of the mitochondrially encoded respiratory-chain subunits is reduced, causing a combined deficiency of the oxidative-phosphorylation complexes. The resulting energy deficit preferentially injures tissues with high and sustained metabolic demand — the long corticospinal and peripheral axons, the optic nerve and, in severe cases, the brainstem and basal ganglia — accounting for the spastic, optic and neuropathic features and, at the severe extreme, Leigh-like decompensation.
additionalDifferentials: SPG7 (paraplegin) — the other classic mitochondrial HSP, which can also show optic atrophy and ophthalmoplegia
Behr syndrome and other childhood optic-atrophy-plus phenotypes
Leigh syndrome and other mitochondrial encephalopathies (including allelic COXPD7)
SPG5 (CYP7B1) and other complicated HSPs with peripheral neuropathy
Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (ARSACS)
additionalInvestigations: MRI brain, which may show cerebellar or optic-pathway atrophy or Leigh-like signal change at the severe end
Nerve conduction studies and EMG to confirm the axonal sensorimotor neuropathy
Ophthalmological assessment with optical coherence tomography and visual evoked potentials for optic atrophy
Blood and, where indicated, cerebrospinal-fluid lactate (may be raised, though a normal value does not exclude the diagnosis)
Genetic testing for C12orf65 / MTRFR, ideally within a mitochondrial or HSP gene panel or exome
Muscle biopsy with respiratory-chain enzyme analysis in selected cases
Echocardiography and other assessments for extra-neural mitochondrial involvement
redFlags: Encephalopathy or developmental regression suggesting Leigh-like metabolic decompensation
Acute deterioration during intercurrent illness or catabolic stress
reference.prognosis: The course is variable and progressive; combined pyramidal, visual and neuropathic disability accumulates over years, and the severe Leigh-like end of the spectrum carries a considerably poorer outlook.
pitfalls: Labelling the child as having Behr syndrome or SPG7 without pursuing C12orf65 / MTRFR testing
Overlooking optic atrophy when spasticity dominates the presentation
Assuming a normal blood lactate rules out a mitochondrial cause
Failing to recognise the mitochondrial basis, which has implications for anaesthesia, avoidance of metabolic stress and family counselling
